Question 1: Boundary and margin

Use margin-geometry-20.csv from the combined ZIP, which contains 20 observations with predictors x1,x2x_1,x_2 and class labels y∈{−1,1}y\in\{-1,1\}. Consider the score

f(x)=0.8x1+0.6x2. f(x)=0.8x_1+0.6x_2.

Since ∥(0.8,0.6)∥2=1\|(0.8,0.6)\|_2=1, the lines f(x)=±1f(x)=\pm1 are each a distance 1 from the decision boundary f(x)=0f(x)=0.

  1. Calculate the distance from every observation to the decision boundary and its functional margin yf(x)yf(x). In a table, report these values and whether each observation is inside, on, or beyond the margin for its class. Compare yf(x)yf(x) with 1 to make this distinction.
d <- read.csv("data/margin-geometry-20.csv")
id_col <- setdiff(names(d), c("x1", "x2", "y"))[1]
d$obs <- if (!is.na(id_col)) d[[id_col]] else seq_len(nrow(d))
d$f <- 0.8 * d$x1 + 0.6 * d$x2
d$distance <- abs(d$f)
d$margin <- d$y * d$f
d$position <- ifelse(abs(d$margin - 1) < 1e-8, "on",
                     ifelse(d$margin < 1, "inside", "beyond"))
tab <- d[, c("obs", "x1", "x2", "y", "f", "distance", "margin", "position")]
names(tab) <- c("Obs", "x1", "x2", "y", "f(x)", "Distance", "y f(x)", "Position")
knitr::kable(tab, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
Obs x1 x2 y f(x) Distance y f(x) Position
1 0.68 0.76 1 1.00 1.00 1.00 on
2 1.80 -0.15 1 1.35 1.35 1.35 beyond
3 1.38 0.66 1 1.50 1.50 1.50 beyond
4 0.88 1.66 1 1.70 1.70 1.70 beyond
5 0.62 2.34 1 1.90 1.90 1.90 beyond
6 2.78 -0.04 1 2.20 2.20 2.20 beyond
7 1.86 1.52 1 2.40 2.40 2.40 beyond
8 0.50 0.40 1 0.64 0.64 0.64 inside
9 0.10 0.20 1 0.20 0.20 0.20 inside
10 -0.40 0.20 1 -0.20 0.20 -0.20 inside
11 -0.92 -0.44 -1 -1.00 1.00 1.00 on
12 -0.50 -1.50 -1 -1.30 1.30 1.30 beyond

The weight vector (0.8, 0.6) has length 1, so the distance from an observation to the boundary is the absolute value of f(x), and the functional margin is y times f(x). An observation is inside the margin if y f(x) is less than 1, on the margin if it equals 1, and beyond the margin if it is greater than 1.

  1. Plot the observations, the boundary f(x)=0f(x)=0, and the margin lines f(x)=±1f(x)=\pm1. Distinguish the two classes and identify the observations inside the margin in your plot.
plot(NA, xlim = c(-3.2, 3.2), ylim = c(-3, 3), asp = 1,
     xlab = "x1", ylab = "x2",
     main = "Observations, boundary f(x) = 0, and margin lines f(x) = +/- 1")
abline(a = 0, b = -0.8 / 0.6, lwd = 2)
abline(a = 1 / 0.6, b = -0.8 / 0.6, lty = 2)
abline(a = -1 / 0.6, b = -0.8 / 0.6, lty = 2)
cols <- ifelse(d$y == 1, "#0072B2", "#D55E00")
shapes <- ifelse(d$y == 1, 19, 17)
points(d$x1, d$x2, col = cols, pch = shapes, cex = 1.2)
inside <- d$position == "inside"
points(d$x1[inside], d$x2[inside], pch = 1, cex = 2.4, lwd = 2)
text(d$x1, d$x2, labels = d$obs, pos = 3, cex = 0.7)
legend("topright",
       legend = c("y = 1", "y = -1", "Inside the margin (ringed)",
                  "Boundary f = 0", "Margin lines f = +/- 1"),
       col = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00", "black", "black", "black"),
       pch = c(19, 17, 1, NA, NA), lty = c(NA, NA, NA, 1, 2),
       lwd = c(NA, NA, 2, 2, 1), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
  1. Report how many observations are inside, on, and beyond the margin. Which observations are misclassified by this decision rule?

Use the observation numbers supplied in the data. Set the x1x_1 axis to [−3.2,3.2][-3.2,3.2], set the x2x_2 axis to [−3,3][-3,3], and use an equal aspect ratio. Do not fit a new classifier for this question.

table(factor(d$position, levels = c("inside", "on", "beyond")))

inside     on beyond 
     6      2     12 
d$obs[d$margin < 0]
[1] 10 20

Of the 20 observations, 6 are inside the margin (y f(x) is below 1), 2 are on the margin (y f(x) equals 1), and 12 are beyond the margin (y f(x) is above 1). Observations 10 and 20 are misclassified by this decision rule: their y f(x) values are negative, which means they lie on the wrong side of the boundary f(x) = 0. Because a negative y f(x) is also less than 1, both of them are counted among the 6 observations inside the margin.

Question 2: Margin in four dimensions

Use margin-geometry-4d.csv from the combined ZIP, which contains 50 observations with four predictors and class labels y∈{−1,1}y\in\{-1,1\}. Consider the linear score

f(𝒙)=β0+𝒙𝖳𝜷,β0=−1,𝜷=(1,2,−2,4)𝖳. f(\mathbf{x})=\beta_0+\mathbf{x}^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol{\beta}, \qquad \beta_0=-1, \quad \boldsymbol{\beta}=(1,2,-2,4)^{\mathsf T}.

  1. Project the observations onto the direction of 𝜷\boldsymbol{\beta} and plot their positions on one axis. Distinguish the two classes and mark the decision boundary. Use the plot to calculate the geometric margin MM, the distance from the boundary to the closest observation.
d4 <- read.csv("data/margin-geometry-4d.csv")
xcols <- grep("^x", names(d4), value = TRUE)
if (length(xcols) != 4) stop("Check column names: ", paste(names(d4), collapse = ", "))
X <- as.matrix(d4[, xcols])
y <- d4$y
beta <- c(1, 2, -2, 4)
beta0 <- -1
norm_beta <- sqrt(sum(beta^2))
t_pos <- as.vector(X %*% beta) / norm_beta
boundary <- -beta0 / norm_beta
gap <- abs(t_pos - boundary)
M <- min(gap)
closest <- which.min(gap)
c(norm_beta = norm_beta, boundary = boundary, M = M, closest_observation = closest)
          norm_beta            boundary                   M closest_observation 
                5.0                 0.2                 1.0                 4.0 
set.seed(1)
jit <- runif(length(t_pos), -0.2, 0.2)
plot(t_pos, jit, col = ifelse(y == 1, "#0072B2", "#D55E00"),
     pch = ifelse(y == 1, 19, 17), ylim = c(-1, 1), yaxt = "n",
     xlab = "Position along the direction of beta (x times beta, divided by 5)",
     ylab = "", main = "Observations projected onto the direction of beta")
abline(v = boundary, lwd = 2)
abline(v = boundary + c(-M, M), lty = 2)
legend("topright", legend = c("y = 1", "y = -1", "Boundary", "Boundary +/- M"),
       col = c("#0072B2", "#D55E00", "black", "black"),
       pch = c(19, 17, NA, NA), lty = c(NA, NA, 1, 2), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)

The vector beta has length 5, so each observation’s position along the direction of beta is t = (x times beta) divided by 5. The boundary f(x) = 0 sits at t = 0.2, since beta0 + 5t = 0 gives t = 1/5. In the plot, the observation closest to the boundary is observation 4, and it sits 1 unit from the boundary. The geometric margin is therefore M = 1, and the dashed lines at 0.2 minus 1 and 0.2 plus 1 mark the edges of the margin. No observation lies inside these dashed lines.

  1. Express the same decision boundary using the SVM normalization in which the smallest functional margin yif(𝒙i)y_i f(\mathbf{x}_i) is set to 1. What are the corresponding values of 𝜷\boldsymbol{\beta} and β0\beta_0?
f <- beta0 + as.vector(X %*% beta)
yf <- y * f
scale_c <- 1 / min(yf)
beta_new <- scale_c * beta
beta0_new <- scale_c * beta0
list(smallest_yf = min(yf), scale = scale_c, beta0 = beta0_new, beta = beta_new,
     check_smallest_yf = min(y * (beta0_new + as.vector(X %*% beta_new))),
     one_over_norm = 1 / sqrt(sum(beta_new^2)))
$smallest_yf
[1] 5

$scale
[1] 0.2

$beta0
[1] -0.2

$beta
[1]  0.2  0.4 -0.4  0.8

$check_smallest_yf
[1] 1

$one_over_norm
[1] 1

The smallest functional margin y f(x) with the original beta and beta0 is 5. Multiplying beta0 and beta by 1/5 makes the smallest functional margin equal to 1 without changing the decision boundary. The result is beta = (0.2, 0.4, -0.4, 0.8) and beta0 = -0.2. The check is consistent: the smallest y f(x) is now 1, and 1 divided by the length of the new beta equals 1, which is the geometric margin M.

Question 3: Peer review of a Homework 7 skill

The instructor’s GitHub account, rqzhu-aide, will open a GitHub Issue in the repository containing your Homework 7 submission. It will link to one assigned student’s repository.

  1. Use the skill. Find the complete skill definition in the assigned student’s Homework 7 report. Copy it without changes into a local SKILL.md file in your own folder. You do not need to install it. Give your agent the path to the file and explicitly ask it to follow that skill while analyzing the SAheart data, using the response and predictor coding from Homework 7. Provide the necessary data information, but no additional preferences about methods, figures, model selection, or report style. Let the skill direct the analysis.

    Monitor the time, your token use, and your weekly quota while the agent works. If the run is taking too long or using your allowance too quickly, you may send a steer message asking the agent to finish immediately, or stop the run and summarize what you observed. A steer message redirects an agent while it is working; learn how to send one in your AI tool before starting.

It took about 3 minutes to create the report. I did not stop it early at any moment and allowed for anything it asked to be changed. I asked the agent this exact prompt: “Follow the skill in homework/week-08/SKILL.md to analyze homework/week-08/data/saheart.csv. The response is chd and the predictors are the other nine variables, with famhist coded 1 for Absent and 2 for Present.”

  1. Write a peer review. Read the student’s submitted report and what the skill produced in your run. Give a brief overall assessment, followed by three major items the author could improve. You may comment on any aspect of the skill or report. For each item, explain what you observed, why it matters, and what you recommend changing. If you stopped the run early, explain where and why. Write the review yourself, without AI assistance.

The three things I think you could change is that the skill should explain what to do when the reserved test set has already been seen, clarify how to report test performance when an independent set is not available, and require verification that every import requirement is satisfied before the report is actually complete.

For when the test set has already been seen, the report says that an earlier version evaluated QDA on a reserved holdout, but then the corrected model did not use that same holdout later on. This is important because it can introduce bias during the model performance. I would just simply add an instruction to stop using a test set if it is compromised and use a new independent test sample instead in order to avoid bias.

For reporting test performance, the report has cross-validation error rates and shows the selected model, but it doesn’t have the final test error. This is important because we need to know how the selected model performs on new data, not just the data that is used to choose it. I would specify that when a valid test error isn’t being used or is not available, the report should say why that is and explain what it is missing in order to be calculated.

For verifying report requirements, the report contains important things like a comparison table, a bar chart, and a selected model, but the final test error requirement isn’t met. Obviously that data point is very important, but the report still could look complete without meeting that requirement like it does in this instance. I would add a final checklist that makes the agent verify every report requirement and identify which requirements have not been met yet.

The report does a good job showing the model comparison and explaining why each method was selected. However, the skill could be slightly improved by adding clearer instructions of what to do when handling specific situations and making sure all requirements are met.

  1. Share your review. Open a GitHub Issue in the assigned student’s Homework 7 repository containing your review. Copy the same review into your Homework 8 submission report and include a link to the GitHub Issue.

Check.
